title: "Vocal character displacement in southern capuchinos"

author: "Marcelo Araya-Salas"

This site contains the analyses of vocal character displacement in southern capuchino seedeaters (*Sporophila* spp.). We evaluate whether songs of different species are more or less divergent where they co-occur, how much each species' song varies across its range, and which species' populations shifted where they live with congeners.

## Analysis reports

The analysis starts with a [data preparation](scripts/0_data_preparation.qmd) report (PCA and pairwise acoustic distances for simple and complex songs), followed by three analysis steps, each run separately for simple and complex songs:

1.  **[Population structure within species](scripts/1_population_structure.qmd).** Are songs of individuals from the same population more similar than songs from different populations, beyond isolation by distance? This shows there is local variation on which sympatry could act. It can only be tested for species sampled in more than one population (hypoxantha and ruficollis); the other species are described.
2.  **[Sympatry and heterospecific distances](scripts/2_sympatry_and_heterospecific_distances.qmd).** Are heterospecific songs more or less different in sympatry than in allopatry (the sympatry-only models)? A dyadic comparison cannot show which species changed.
3.  **[Population shifts](scripts/3_population_shifts.qmd).** Within a focal species, are populations that co-occur with a congener shifted towards (convergence) or away from (divergence) that congener's song, compared with conspecific populations that do not co-occur with it?

Step 3 can only be tested for hypoxantha and ruficollis relative to each other, because iberaensis and palustris were recorded at a single locality. It rests on very few populations per contrast (2 vs. 2 for ruficollis, 1 vs. 2 for hypoxantha), and single-site contrasts are confounded with anything else particular to that locality. It is therefore presented as supporting evidence, and the size of any co-occurrence shift is compared with ordinary between-population differences.

## Main results

-   **Population structure (Step 1).** Simple songs are population-structured in both testable species, more strongly and more pervasively in *Ruficollis* (credible in all 8 individual acoustic features) than in *Hypoxantha* (credible mainly in spectral/element-level features, not temporal pacing). Complex songs show little to no structuring in *Hypoxantha* (confined almost entirely to element-level acoustic detail) and weaker, patchier structuring than simple songs in *Ruficollis*. Neither song type shows the expected isolation-by-distance signal overall; where a credible slope exists, it runs in the opposite direction — simple-song *Ruficollis* populations that are geographically farther apart are acoustically *more* similar, a pattern that recurs across 7 of 8 individual features, making a neutral-drift explanation for this species' population structure unlikely.
-   **Sympatry (Step 2).** Simple heterospecific songs are credibly more divergent in sympatry than in allopatry — the pattern predicted by sound-based character displacement — and this holds for 7 of 8 individual acoustic features, several of which (element diversity, frequency range, element-level acoustic distance) show effects roughly double the overall PCA-based model. Complex songs show the same direction of effect overall but far weaker, and the per-feature breakdown there is a mosaic rather than a uniform shift. In both song types, however, peak frequency and song rate specifically *converge* rather than diverge in sympatry — the same two features behave the same way in both simple and complex songs, pointing to convergent selection on those particular traits (e.g. shared habitat acoustics or interspecific signalling) acting alongside divergence in most other traits.
-   **Population shifts (Step 3).** No credible population-level shifts (convergence or divergence) were detected for either song type. Only one species pair (*Hypoxantha* vs. *Ruficollis*) has enough co-occurrence structure to test, so this null result reflects very limited statistical power rather than evidence against a shift.
-   Overall, the clearest and best-supported evidence for character displacement in this system is the simple-song sympatry effect in Step 2, reinforced by a largely consistent per-feature signal. Complex songs and the population-shift framing provide weaker, more qualified support, and the recurring convergence in peak frequency and song rate across both song types suggests a secondary, opposite-direction process acting specifically on those two traits.

*Ruficollis* (right panel) is credible and negative for every feature. *Hypoxantha* (left panel) is credible and negative for the spectral/element-level features (`elm_pca`, `freqrange`, `mst`, `numelms`); `gapduration` and `meanpeakf` are also credible but tiny and in the *opposite* direction (between-population pairs very slightly more similar); only `songduration` and `songrate` are not credible (95% CI includes zero). See [Step 1](scripts/1_population_structure.qmd) for the isolation-by-distance results and the complex-song version of this figure.

![Same plot for complex songs. Note the much larger x-axis range, driven by the element-level PCA distance (`elm_pca`).](index_files/figure-html/step2 figure complex-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Both song types show the same two-feature exception to an otherwise mostly-divergent pattern: `meanpeakf` and `songrate` are the only features with a credibly *negative* sympatry effect in both plots, while most other features (and the overall `acoustic (PCA)` distance) are credibly positive. For complex songs, `elm_pca` stands out as far larger than everything else, including the overall PCA-based distance — the element-level signal is diluted when averaged into the whole-song measure. See [Step 2](scripts/2_sympatry_and_heterospecific_distances.qmd) for species-pair-level detail and full model diagnostics.

:::

## Reproducibility

All code and data are available in the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/maRce10/vocal_character_displacement_in_southern_capuchinos). See the repository README for the folder structure and for files not hosted on GitHub.
